---
title: "Naming"
---

```{python}
#| label: setup-naming
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: the imports every example on this page uses"
#| output: false
import polars as pl

import dagster_dataframely as dd
from dagster_dataframely.data import OrdersSchema
```

From the schema, `dd.asset` sets the asset's description, fills the Columns tab, and names and describes each check.
To change the text the Dagster UI shows, find its source below, and edit that docstring, rule or argument.
The page also covers the op name that Dagster builds from the asset key, and the three namespaces this package reserves.

## The description comes from the schema

`dd.asset` takes the asset's description from the first of these you set: the `description=` argument, the schema's docstring, and the decorated function's docstring, which is Dagster's own default.

```{python}
#| label: naming-1
@dd.asset(OrdersSchema)
def orders() -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Join the two extracts and drop the test accounts."""
    ...


orders.get_asset_spec().description
```

The schema's docstring takes precedence over the function's, because it describes the table, not the code.
Assets that share a schema share its description, and `description=` gives one of them its own.
`dd.asset` reads the schema's own docstring only, and ignores one inherited from a parent class, including `dy.Schema`'s.

The spec from `build_error_rows_spec` has its own description: `Rows from <asset> that failed an 'error' rule, with one column per rule.`

## Where a check's text comes from

The Dagster UI shows a schema's rules in three places, and the table lists the sources of each in order.

| place | first choice | then | then |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Columns tab | the rendered column constraint | the rule name | never the docstring |
| check name | `dy_rule__<rule>` at `rule` granularity, `dy_col__<column>` or `dy_rule__<rule>` for a schema-level rule at `column` granularity | never the docstring | |
| check description | the rule's docstring | `<column> <rendered constraint>`, with the rule's expression after a `check=` key | the whole name Dataframely reports, column part included, and the rule's expression |
| collapsed check description | each rule's rendered constraint, with the rule's expression after a `check=` key | the rule name and the rule's expression | never the docstring |

A check description shows the rule's Polars expression as a code span after a `check=` key, `custom check` or a rule name, because these do not show what the rule tests.
At `rule` granularity, `dy_rule__email__check__lowercase` has the description `` email lowercase `[(col("email").str.to_lowercase()) == (col("email"))]` ``.
A rendered constraint such as `>= 1` already shows what the rule tests, so it appears without the expression.
A rule's docstring appears without it too.

Dataframely builds a `@dy.rule()` expression by calling its function.
`dd.asset` builds every rule's expression to derive the [code version](declaring-an-asset.qmd#the-code-version), so a function that raises raises where you declare the asset, not when it runs.
With your own `code_version`, `dd.asset` builds an expression only for a description that shows it.

A rule's value, such as the bound of `min`, appears in the column constraint, the check description and the check result's metadata, but never in the check name.
So changing a bound does not rename the check or start a new check history.

The package renders column constraints as operators: `>= 0.0`, `length <= 64 bytes`, `matches ^[a-z]+$`, `in (a, b)`, `aligned to 1h`.
It omits `nullability` and `unique`, because Dagster has separate fields for them on the column.
It omits `inf` and `nan` too, because Dataframely adds them to every float column by default.
Each of the four still has its own check at `rule` granularity, and a collapsed check's description lists it at `column` granularity.

Dataframely names a bare `check=` lambda `check`, which does not show what it tests.
The package renders it as `custom check`, in the Columns tab and before the expression in a check description.
Name your checks with a dict, such as `check={"lowercase": ...}`, and the package shows the key instead.

## Dagster names the op after the whole asset key

`@dd.asset(OrdersSchema, key_prefix="sales", name="orders")` creates an op named `sales__orders`, the same way `@dg.asset` names its op.

The op name is also the step key and the key under `ops:` in run config, so both use the whole asset key:

```yaml
ops:
  sales__orders:
    config:
      threshold: 4
```

## The reserved namespaces

This package reserves three namespaces: `dy_`, `dataframely/` and `<name>__error_rows`.

**`dy_`** starts every check name and every rule column in the error rows.
The check names are the column-schema check `dy_schema__columns`, each rule's check `dy_rule__<rule>`, the collapsed checks `dy_col__<column>`, and each collection filter's check `dy_filter__<name>`.
A collapsed check's failure examples also have a `dy_rule` column, which names the rule each row failed.

A rule's check name is `dy_rule__` plus the name Dataframely gives the rule, with `|` replaced by `__`: `amount|min` becomes `dy_rule__amount__min`.
`dd.wiring.get_check_name_for_rule("amount|min")` returns that check name, so a test does not have to build it by hand.

A collection filter's check name is `dy_filter__` plus the collection filter's name, as [Collection checks](collection-checks.qmd) shows.

**`dataframely/`** starts every metadata key this package names, on a materialization, a definition or a check result.
A check result can have `dataframely/rule`, `dataframely/rule_expr`, `dataframely/rules`, `dataframely/filter`, `dataframely/failed_row_count`, `dataframely/failed_examples`, `dataframely/column_schema_errors` and `dataframely/error_rows_address`.

Every public function that takes a schema raises three errors for names this package cannot use ([ADR-0008](https://github.com/ozanozbeker/dagster-dataframely/blob/main/docs/pre-1.0.md#adr-0008-every-public-function-that-takes-a-schema-validates-it)).
It raises `ReservedColumnError` for a column name that starts with `dy_`.
It raises `InvalidColumnNameError` for a column name with characters Dagster does not allow in a check name, which is anything outside `A-Za-z0-9_`.
It raises `CheckNameCollisionError` for two rules that produce the same check name.
So `dd.asset` raises them where you declare the asset, and a hand-wired asset raises them in the first of these functions it calls.

A column name with such characters almost always comes from `dy.Column(alias=...)`, which Dataframely provides for a name that is not a Python identifier.
A `|` is one of them, and Dataframely also uses it to separate a column from its rule name.

**`<name>__error_rows`** is the third: the default error-rows key, which a writer writes the error rows under.
You also choose asset keys in this key space, so another asset can already have this key.
A run raises `ErrorRowsKeyCollisionError` when another asset materializes this key, as [Errors](errors.qmd#common-mistakes) describes.

No setting or argument changes `dy_` or `dataframely/`.
`error_rows_key` replaces the third for one asset, as [Filtering error rows](filtering-error-rows.qmd#two-keywords-change-the-key-and-the-io-manager) describes.
